title: A Letter to God
short: Lencho's unshakable faith and the irony that follows it.
lede: G. L. Fuentes. A farmer, a hailstorm, a letter — and one of the sharpest ironies in the syllabus.
lens: Reference-to-context extracts and one 5-mark value-based long answer. The **irony** is always the question.
Know the numbers cold: Lencho asked for **one hundred pesos**, received **seventy**, and accused the post office employees of being *'a bunch of crooks'*.
concepts: **1. Summary.** Lencho, a simple hardworking farmer, lives on the crest of a low hill in a Latin American valley, with his cornfield ripening and dotted with flowers. Rain comes — but it turns into a **hailstorm** that destroys the crop completely. Lencho's only hope is God, so he writes a letter asking for one hundred pesos to sow his field again and to live until the next harvest. The postmaster, a fat, amiable fellow, is moved by the farmer's faith, collects **seventy pesos** from his employees and friends, and sends the money in a letter signed *'God'*. Lencho, on receiving the letter, is not surprised, but is angry at the shortfall: he writes a second letter asking God to send the rest directly, because the post office employees are a bunch of crooks.

**2. Characters.** **Lencho** — a simple, hardworking, unquestioning man of faith; his faith is absolute but so is his innocence. **The postmaster** — kind, generous and witty; he does not want to shake the farmer's faith in God. **The employees and friends of the post office** — they contribute out of charity, and are unjustly called crooks.

**3. Themes.** **Unshakable faith** — Lencho never doubts that God will answer. **Irony** — the very people who helped him are the ones he calls crooks. **Human kindness and generosity** — the postmaster's act is not duty but compassion. **The gap between faith and reality.**
tricks: - The word **'crooks'** in the last line is the exam favourite. It means dishonest people — and the irony is that Lencho says it about the men who gave him money.
- **Two ironies, not one:** the hailstorm destroys the crop that the rain was supposed to save; and the helpers are accused of theft.
- Lencho is *not* grateful in the second letter — that surprise is worth a mark.
mistakes: - Saying Lencho received one hundred pesos. He received **seventy**.
- Describing the postmaster as Lencho's relative or a government official on duty. He acted **out of personal kindness**.
- Missing the word **'amiable'** when describing the postmaster — examiners look for textual detail.

qa.q: Why did Lencho say the post office employees were a bunch of crooks?
qa.a: Because he had asked God for one hundred pesos and received only seventy. His faith was so absolute that he could not believe God had made a mistake or had sent less, so he concluded that the post office employees must have taken the remaining thirty pesos. The irony is that these were the very men who had collected the money for him out of charity.

qa.q: What made the postmaster decide to help Lencho?
qa.a: He was moved by the farmer's unshakable faith in God. He did not want to shake that faith, so he collected money from his employees and friends, gave part of his own salary, and sent it to Lencho in a letter signed 'God'.

qa.q: Was Lencho surprised to find a letter with money in it? What made him angry?
qa.a: No, he was not surprised at all — he had expected an answer from God, and his confidence in God was so complete that receiving a reply seemed natural. What made him angry was that the envelope contained only seventy pesos instead of the hundred he had asked for. He was certain that God could not have made a mistake, so he concluded that the post office employees had taken the rest.

qa.q: A student writes: “Lencho received one hundred pesos from God and thanked Him.” Correct this using the text.
a: Lencho asked for a hundred pesos but received only **seventy**; the money had been collected by the postmaster from his employees and friends, plus part of his own salary.
He was not surprised to get a reply, since he was sure God would answer, but he became angry when he counted the money.
He then wrote a second letter asking God to send the rest, and not by post, because the post-office employees were “a bunch of crooks”.

qa.q: Lencho never thanks the postmaster or his helpers. Is he being fair to them? Give two reasons.
a: No. The postmaster and his employees gave their own money to help a stranger, and Lencho accuses them of stealing the missing thirty pesos.
His faith in God is so complete that he cannot imagine ordinary people being generous, so he credits God alone and suspects men.
His mistake comes from innocence, not cruelty; this is what makes the ending ironic.

qa.q: Bring out the irony in the ending of ‘A Letter to God'.
qa.a: Lencho is certain that God sent him the money and cannot imagine that human beings could be so generous. He writes a second letter to complain and calls the post office employees ‘a bunch of crooks' because thirty pesos were missing. The irony is that the very people who helped him are the ones he distrusts: his faith in God survives, while his faith in human beings is destroyed.

qa.q: “The postmaster was a fat, jolly fellow.” How does his character contrast with Lencho's, and why does the contrast matter to the story?
a: Lencho is intense, single-minded and absolute in his faith; the postmaster is warm, practical and humane — he helps without needing to be believed in.
The contrast creates the story's deepest irony: the believer cannot recognise human kindness, while the kind man asks for no recognition at all.
Without this contrast the ending would be merely sad; with it, it becomes a comment on faith that blinds as well as sustains.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

After a gentle rain, large hailstones began to fall on Lencho’s valley. He said they looked like new coins. Soon the field was white, as if covered with salt, and he said a plague of locusts would have left more than the hail had.

(a) What did the hailstones first look like to Lencho?
(b) What do the white field and the locusts tell us about the damage?
(c) Where did Lencho turn for hope, and why?
a: (a) They looked like new silver coins, which at first seemed like a blessing.
(b) The crop was completely destroyed, even worse than a plague of locusts would have left it, so the family faced hunger for the year.
(c) To God, because his faith was unshakable and he believed that no one else could help.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

The postmaster read Lencho’s letter to God.

(a) How did he react at first?
(b) What changed his attitude?
(c) What did he do to help, and how did he hide it?
a: (a) He laughed.
(b) He became serious when he realised how deep the writer’s faith was; he did not want to shake it.
(c) He collected money from his employees and friends and gave part of his own salary, and sent it in an envelope with a letter signed “God”.

qa.q: Describe Lencho's character and say what his faith tells us about him.
a: Lencho is a poor but hard-working farmer who knows his field like a child and never stops hoping for a good crop.
His faith is complete and childlike: after the hailstorm destroys everything, he writes to God for a hundred pesos with the same confidence with which he sows his field.
The same faith makes him naive — he cannot imagine that the postmaster and his staff collected the money themselves.
The story uses this innocence to show both the strength of faith and the loneliness of the poor, who trust God more than the people around them.

qa.q: 'The story is built around two ironies.' Explain with reference to the text.
a: The first irony is in the weather: Lencho's field needed rain, and rain did come — but it turned into a hailstorm that destroyed the entire crop. The very thing that promised a good harvest took it away.

The second irony is in the ending: the post office employees, moved by Lencho's faith, collected seventy pesos and sent them to him. Lencho, finding the amount short, wrote back accusing those same men of stealing the money and calling them 'a bunch of crooks'. The helpers become the accused thieves, and the man who never doubted God doubts the honesty of human beings.

qa.q: What does “A Letter to God” suggest about faith and human kindness? Discuss with reference to Lencho and the postmaster.
a: Lencho’s faith is complete: after the hail he writes to God as confidently as he sowed his field.
The postmaster represents human goodness: he acts out of kindness and asks for no thanks.
The irony is that Lencho keeps his faith in God but loses his faith in people, accusing the helpers of cheating him.
The story shows that faith is admirable, yet it can blind a person to the real kindness around him.
It also suggests that God’s help can reach us through human hands.

mcq.q: Lencho asked God for: (a) fifty pesos (b) seventy pesos (c) one hundred pesos (d) one hundred and fifty pesos
mcq.a: **(c) one hundred pesos**, to sow his field again and to live until the coming harvest.

mcq.q: The letter Lencho received was signed: (a) the postmaster (b) God (c) the employees of the post office (d) the President
mcq.a: **(b) God** — the postmaster signed it that way so that Lencho's faith would not be shaken.

mcq.q: The writer of the story 'A Letter to God' is: (a) G. L. Fuentes (b) Nelson Mandela (c) Liam O'Flaherty (d) Betty Renshaw
mcq.a: **(a) G. L. Fuentes.**

mcq.q: When the postmaster first read Lencho’s letter, he: (a) tore it up (b) gave it to the police (c) ignored it (d) laughed, and then became serious
mcq.a: **(d) laughed, and then became serious.** He laughed at the idea of a letter to God, but Lencho’s faith moved him and he decided to answer it.

mcq.q: In his second letter, Lencho described the post-office employees as: (a) kind-hearted men (b) a bunch of crooks (c) God’s messengers (d) his relatives
mcq.a: **(b) a bunch of crooks.** He believed they had kept the missing thirty pesos, though they had actually collected the seventy.

mcq.q: Lencho asked God for: (a) 30 pesos  (b) 70 pesos  (c) 100 pesos  (d) 1000 pesos
mcq.a: **(c) 100 pesos.** He asked for a hundred pesos to sow his field again and live until the harvest.

mcq.q: The postmaster and his staff managed to collect: (a) 100 pesos  (b) 70 pesos  (c) 30 pesos  (d) 700 pesos
mcq.a: **(b) 70 pesos.** They contributed from their own salaries, and the postmaster put in the rest of his own money.

mcq.q: The postmaster collected the seventy pesos by: (a) asking the government (b) giving part of his salary and asking employees and friends (c) borrowing from a bank (d) selling his watch
mcq.a: **(b) giving part of his salary and asking employees and friends.** The money was charity collected peso by peso.

trend: The two ironies and the 'bunch of crooks' line are asked in almost every paper; the postmaster's character is the recurring short answer.
onepager: - Lencho: simple farmer, hailstorm destroys the corn, writes to God for 100 pesos.
- Postmaster collects 70 pesos, signs the letter 'God'.
- Lencho is not surprised by the letter, only angry at the shortfall.
- Two ironies: the rain that destroyed, and the helpers called crooks.
task: Write the story in five sentences, then rewrite it from the postmaster's point of view in five sentences. The shift in perspective shows you who the real subject of the story is — and it is not Lencho.
steps: 1. Name the **place, the crop and the disaster** first — Lencho's field of ripe corn on a hilltop, destroyed by hail.
2. State what Lencho does next and why it matters: he writes to God for **100 pesos**, which shows his unshakeable faith.
3. Describe the **postmaster's response** — he collects money from his staff so that Lencho's faith is not shaken.
4. Close with the **irony**: Lencho calls them 'a bunch of crooks' because only 70 pesos arrived — the story's turning point.

title: Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom
short: Apartheid, the inauguration of 1994 and what freedom came to mean.
lede: An extract from Mandela's autobiography *Long Walk to Freedom*. Dates and definitions carry the marks.
lens: Reference-to-context extracts and one 5-mark long answer on the meaning of freedom or on courage.
**10 May 1994** — the inauguration at the Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria — is the anchor date.
Know the three national anthems, the meaning of **apartheid**, and the two obligations.
concepts: **1. Summary.** On **10 May 1994**, Nelson Mandela was sworn in as South Africa's first black President at the **Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria**, before an international gathering of leaders. The day marked the end of **apartheid** — a political system that separated people according to race — and the birth of a new, democratic, non-racial nation. **Three national anthems** were sung: *'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika'* and *'Morena'* by the blacks, *'Die Stem'* the old anthem of the Republic, and the new combined anthem. Mandela reflects on the day: a beautiful autumn day, but for the whites a symbol of victory and for the blacks a symbol of a new beginning. He recalls his own journey from a frightened young man to a bold one, and thanks the **international presence**, which he sees as a common victory for justice, peace and human dignity.

**2. Courage and oppression.** Mandela says that he learned that **courage was not the absence of fear but the triumph over it** — the brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear. Decades of oppression made him hunger for freedom, not just for himself but for all his people. He says that **the oppressed and the oppressor alike are robbed of their humanity**: the oppressor is a prisoner of hatred, locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness, and is not truly free; the oppressed, robbed of his dignity, is also not free.

**3. The twin obligations.** Every man has **two obligations**: the first to his **family** — his parents, his wife and children; the second to his **people**, his community and his country. In a civil and humane society each man is able to fulfil both. In South Africa under apartheid, a man like Mandela who tried to live as a human being was **punished and isolated**, and could not fulfil either obligation.

**4. The meaning of freedom.** As a boy, freedom meant running in the fields, swimming in the stream and roasting mealies under the stars. As a student, it meant staying out at night, reading what he pleased and going where he liked — **transitory freedoms**. As a young man he yearned for the honourable freedoms of achieving his potential, of earning his keep, of marrying and having a family. Only later did he understand that **freedom is indivisible** — the chains on any one of his people were chains on all of them. He says that freedom was not just to throw off one's chains, but **to live in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others**. His long walk is not yet ended.
tricks: - **Courage = triumph over fear, not absence of fear.** That sentence is asked repeatedly and must be quoted nearly word-for-word.
- **Two obligations: family and people.** In apartheid South Africa, a man could not discharge both.
- **Freedom changed meaning with age:** boyhood = physical freedom, youth = honourable freedoms, later = freedom of the whole people.
mistakes: - Giving the inauguration date as 10 May 1995. It is **1994**.
- Saying South Africa has two national anthems. **Three** were sung that day.
- Defining apartheid as segregation only. The textbook calls it a **political system that separates people according to race**.

qa.q: What does courage mean to Mandela?
qa.a: For Mandela, courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it. The brave man is not the one who does not feel afraid, but the one who conquers that fear. He says he felt fear more times than he can remember, and it was this repeated conquest of fear that made him bold.

qa.q: What 'twin obligations' does Mandela mention?
qa.a: The first obligation is to his family — his parents, his wife and children. The second is to his people, his community and his country. In a civil and humane society each person can fulfil both, but in South Africa under apartheid, a man like Mandela who tried to live as a human being was punished and isolated, and could not discharge either obligation.

qa.q: Why did such a large number of international leaders attend the inauguration? What did it signify?
qa.a: It signified the recognition by the international community of the birth of a free, democratic, non-racial South Africa, and a common victory for justice, for peace and for human dignity. The presence of leaders of many nations showed that the end of apartheid was not only a South African event but a triumph of values shared by the whole world.

qa.q: Why does Mandela say that the oppressor is also not free?
qa.a: Because the oppressor is a prisoner of hatred, locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness. A man who takes away another man's freedom is himself deprived of his own humanity, so the oppressor and the oppressed are both robbed of what makes them human.

qa.q: A student writes that Mandela’s inauguration took place on 10 May 1995 and that apartheid simply meant keeping races apart. Correct both statements.
a: The inauguration took place on **10 May 1994**, in the amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria.
Apartheid was a system of racial discrimination: laws separated people by race and denied the black majority their freedom and rights.
Under it, a man who tried to live as a free human being could be punished and isolated.

qa.q: Mandela says, “Courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it.” Give an example from school life that fits this idea and explain why.
a: Courage means acting rightly in spite of feeling afraid.
Example: a student who is terrified of public speaking, yet takes part in a debate. She is brave because she feels the fear and still goes ahead.
In the same way, Mandela felt fear many times but conquered it, and that is what made him brave.

qa.q: What does Mandela mean when he says that freedom is indivisible?
qa.a: He means that no one is truly free while others are unfree: the oppressor is as much a prisoner of hatred as the oppressed is of chains. His own hunger for freedom for his people was what made him lose the freedom to live with his family, and this cannot be separated from the freedom of every South African, white or black.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

In his speech Mandela said, “Never, never and never again shall it be that this beautiful land will again experience the oppression of one by another.”

(a) On what occasion did he say this?
(b) What is the effect of repeating “never”?
(c) What does “the oppression of one by another” refer to?
a: (a) At his inauguration as the first black President of South Africa, on 10 May 1994.
(b) The repetition adds force and shows a firm, solemn promise that the past will not return.
(c) The system of apartheid, in which one racial group dominated and oppressed the others.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Mandela remembers his boyhood as a time when he was “born free”: running in the fields near his mother’s hut, swimming in a clear stream and roasting mealies under the stars. Later he calls this freedom an illusion.

(a) Name two of the freedoms of his boyhood.
(b) Why does he call them an illusion?
(c) What did he begin to hunger for as a young man?
a: (a) Any two: running in the fields, swimming in the stream, roasting mealies, riding the backs of bulls.
(b) He found that, as a black South African, his basic freedom had already been taken away by the laws of apartheid.
(c) The freedom of his people to live with dignity and to achieve their potential.

qa.q: Describe the inauguration of 10 May 1994 and the obligations Mandela spoke of.
a: The ceremony took place in the amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria, watched by leaders and citizens of many countries and by a crowd of South Africans.
Mandela was sworn in as the first black President of a democratic South Africa, with Thabo Mbeki and de Klerk as his deputies, and the old and new national anthems were sung.
He spoke of the courage of the people, of the end of white rule and of the birth of a society in which all would be equal.
He said the obligation of the new government was to free the people from poverty, deprivation, suffering, gender and other discrimination, so that the dignity of every person is respected.

qa.q: How did Mandela's understanding of freedom change with age and experience?
a: **As a boy** in the villages of Umtata, freedom meant being able to run in the fields near his mother's hut, to swim in the stream, to roast mealies under the stars and to ride the broad backs of slow-moving bulls. It was the freedom of a child, and it seemed boundless.
**As a student** he wanted the transitory freedoms of staying out at night, reading what he pleased and going where he liked.
**As a young man** he yearned for the honourable freedoms — of achieving his potential, of earning his keep, of marrying and having a family, of living lawfully in a law-abiding society.

**Later** he realised that these were only illusory, because he was not free and neither were his people. He came to understand that **freedom is indivisible**: the chains on any one of his people were chains on all of them. He saw that the oppressed and the oppressor alike are robbed of their humanity, and that freedom is not merely to throw off one's chains but to live in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others.

qa.q: What kind of South Africa did Mandela promise at his inauguration, and what values did he stress?
a: He promised a society in which all South Africans, black and white, could walk tall without fear, assured of their human dignity: a “rainbow nation”.
He said that the new government would never allow one group to oppress another again.
He paid tribute to the courage of ordinary people who had resisted apartheid.
He spoke of the twin obligations to family and to one’s people, and said freedom is **indivisible**: the oppressor and the oppressed must both be freed.
His speech joined the personal and the national, showing that freedom, to be real, must be shared by everyone.

mcq.q: Mandela was sworn in as South Africa's first black President on: (a) 10 May 1994 (b) 10 May 1995 (c) 26 April 1994 (d) 27 April 1993
mcq.a: **(a) 10 May 1994**, at the Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria.

mcq.q: How many national anthems were sung at the inauguration? (a) one (b) two (c) three (d) four
mcq.a: **(c) three** — 'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika' and 'Morena' by the blacks, 'Die Stem' the old anthem, and the new combined anthem.

mcq.q: According to Mandela, courage is: (a) the absence of fear (b) the triumph over fear (c) the denial of pain (d) the love of danger
mcq.a: **(b) the triumph over fear** — the brave man conquers fear rather than not feeling it.

mcq.q: Mandela’s inauguration took place in the amphitheatre formed by the: (a) Parliament House in Cape Town (b) Robben Island prison (c) Johannesburg Stadium (d) Union Buildings in Pretoria
mcq.a: **(d) Union Buildings in Pretoria.** The ceremony was held at the Union Buildings, the seat of government in Pretoria.

mcq.q: According to Mandela, courage is: (a) the absence of fear (b) anger at one’s enemies (c) a gift that few people are born with (d) the triumph over fear, not the absence of fear
mcq.a: **(d) the triumph over fear, not the absence of fear.** He says the brave man is not the one who does not feel afraid but the one who conquers that fear.

mcq.q: The policy of racial discrimination followed in South Africa was called: (a) apartheid  (b) satyagraha  (c) segregation by choice  (d) democracy
mcq.a: **(a) apartheid.** It kept the black majority out of government, jobs, land and even public places.

mcq.q: Mandela's autobiography is titled: (a) Long Walk to Freedom  (b) The Struggle Is My Life  (c) The Prison Diary  (d) Invictus
mcq.a: **(a) Long Walk to Freedom.** The extract in the textbook is taken from it.

mcq.q: Mandela says the oppressor is not free because: (a) he is in prison (b) he is a prisoner of hatred and prejudice (c) he is poor (d) he is uneducated
mcq.a: **(b) he is a prisoner of hatred and prejudice.** The oppressor is robbed of his humanity as surely as the oppressed.

trend: The meaning of freedom and how it changed with age is the set 5-mark answer; the twin obligations and the definition of courage recur as short answers.
onepager: - 10 May 1994, Union Buildings, Pretoria; three anthems; end of apartheid.
- Courage = triumph over fear.
- Twin obligations: family and people; apartheid made both impossible.
- Freedom is indivisible; freedom means living in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others.
task: Write the four stages of Mandela's idea of freedom as four headed sentences (boyhood, student, young man, mature). Practise it once from memory — this is a guaranteed long answer and the headings alone carry two marks.
steps: 1. Give the **date and the setting** — 10 May 1994, the Union Buildings in Pretoria, the first democratic inauguration.
2. Define the ideas in Mandela's own words: **freedom is indivisible**, and the oppressor is as unfree as the oppressed.
3. Trace the three stages of his awareness in **order**: personal freedom → freedom of his people → the courage of others.
4. End with the **'twin obligations'** — to his family, his people and his country — and the line about the 'depths of oppression' creating 'heights of character'.

title: Two Stories about Flying
short: His First Flight by O'Flaherty and The Black Aeroplane by Forsyth.
lede: Two stories, one theme: fear overcome. The seagull is the more frequently examined of the two.
lens: Extracts come from either story; know both well enough to identify which one is quoted.
**His First Flight** — Liam O'Flaherty, a young seagull afraid to fly. **The Black Aeroplane** — Frederick Forsyth, a pilot in a storm helped by a mysterious black aeroplane.
concepts: **1. His First Flight — summary.** A young seagull is alone on his ledge, afraid to fly, while his two brothers and sister have already flown away the day before. His parents have scolded him and threatened to let him starve on the ledge unless he flies. His siblings taunt him by calling him 'Ga-ga'. After **twenty-four hours** of hunger and fear, his mother tears a piece of fish and stands on the ledge, and the sight of the food maddens him. He dives at her, his hunger overcomes his fear, and he falls outward into space. The air rushes against his feathers, he flaps his wings and finds himself soaring. His family screams around him, praising him and offering scraps of fish. He then flies with them, sinks tired onto the water, and though afraid at first, learns to float — his **first flight is complete**.

**2. The Black Aeroplane — summary.** The narrator, flying an old Dakota aeroplane from France to England to spend a breakfast of bacon and eggs with his family, flies into a storm. The clouds are black, his compass and radio fail, and he has only enough fuel for five or ten minutes. He sees a **black aeroplane** with no lights on its wings, and the pilot waves for him to follow. He follows it through the storm until he runs out of fuel, and then the black plane disappears. He lands safely and asks the woman in the control centre where the other pilot is. She says the sky was empty — **there was no other aeroplane** that night, and no other plane on the radar. The narrator looks up and wonders who helped him.

**3. Common theme.** Both stories are about **facing fear and finding the strength to overcome it**. The seagull is helped by hunger and by his mother's example; the pilot is helped — or so he believes — by another pilot. Both suggest that the help we need is sometimes already within us.
tricks: - **Twenty-four hours** on the ledge is the key number in *His First Flight*.
- The seagull's fear breaks when he sees the **fish**, not when his parents scold him.
- In *The Black Aeroplane*, the control-centre woman says there was **no other plane** — that ambiguity is the point of the ending.
mistakes: - Confusing the two authors: **O'Flaherty** wrote *His First Flight*, **Forsyth** wrote *The Black Aeroplane*.
- Saying the seagull flew because his father threatened him. It was **hunger and the sight of food**.
- Naming the Dakota a fighter plane. It is an **old Dakota** carrying the narrator home.

qa.q: Why was the young seagull afraid to fly? What compelled him to finally make the flight?
qa.a: He was afraid because he felt certain that his wings would never support him, and because his siblings had already flown while he was left behind on the ledge. What compelled him to fly was hunger: when his mother tore a piece of fish and stood on the ledge, the sight of the food maddened him, and he dived at it. In that dive he fell outward into space and, flapping his wings, found that he could fly.

qa.q: Describe the help the pilot received during the storm in 'The Black Aeroplane'.
qa.a: When his instruments failed and he ran low on fuel, he saw a black aeroplane with no lights on its wings. Its pilot waved to him and led him through the storm until the narrator came out of the clouds and could see the runway. When he landed and asked the woman in the control centre about the other pilot, she told him there had been no other aeroplane in the sky that night, and no other plane on her radar.

qa.q: How did the seagull's family react when he flew for the first time?
qa.a: They screamed around him, praising him and offering him scraps of fish. They landed ahead of him on the water, beckoning him to join them, and when he finally sank tired onto the sea and floated, they praised him again — his first flight was complete.

qa.q: A student writes that the young seagull flew because his father threatened him. Correct this with evidence from the story.
a: It was **hunger**, not a threat, that made him fly.
His parents and brothers had coaxed and taunted him, but he stayed frozen on the ledge.
When his mother flew by with a piece of fish and stopped just out of reach, he was so hungry that he dived at it, and in the dive his wings opened and he found himself flying.

qa.q: A friend refuses to try swimming after one bad experience. Using the young seagull’s experience, give her three pieces of advice.
a: Fear often comes from imagining that we cannot do something; the seagull was sure his wings would not hold him, yet they did.
A small push or a good reason can help us take the first step; in the story it was hunger.
Once we begin, the fear passes quickly, as it did for the seagull, so she should try again with someone supportive.

qa.q: How did the young seagull finally overcome his fear of flying?
a: His family taunted and cajoled him, but he was too afraid to leave the ledge.
When his mother flew past him with a piece of fish in her beak and stopped just out of reach, the pang of hunger was stronger than his fear.
He dived at the fish, lost his balance, and his wings spread and lifted him automatically.
His fear lasted only a moment; once in the air he was flying, and his parents and brothers praised him.

qa.q: Compare the mother's role in ‘His First Flight’ with the black aeroplane pilot's role. How is each a guide who appears at the right moment?
a: The mother tempts the seagull with fish and then stops short, forcing him to cross the gap between fear and flight — she guides by testing.
The unknown pilot appears when the narrator's instruments fail and his fuel runs low, leading him through the storm to safety — he guides by rescuing.
Both appear at the exact moment when the frightened one must move forward, and both vanish once courage takes over.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

The seagull’s parents and brothers coaxed and scolded him, and his mother finally held a piece of fish out of his reach.

(a) Why did the mother hold the food out of reach?
(b) What effect did hunger have on the seagull?
(c) Do you approve of the family’s method? Why?
a: (a) She wanted to tempt him to leave the ledge; he could get the fish only by flying.
(b) It was stronger than his fear, so he dived at the fish and began to fly.
(c) An answer with a reason: for example, it worked because gentle persuasion had failed, though it was a harsh push for a frightened young bird.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Over the storm, the pilot’s instruments failed and his fuel ran low. Then a black aeroplane appeared in front of him.

(a) How would you describe the pilot’s state of mind?
(b) Which two details increase the tension?
(c) What finally brought him to safety?
a: (a) Anxious and frightened, but hopeful once he saw the other plane.
(b) The failure of his instruments in the storm and the shortage of fuel.
(c) He followed the black aeroplane, which led him through the clouds until he saw the runway.

qa.q: Who do you think was in the black aeroplane? Give reasons for your answer.
a: The pilot saw no lights, no other plane and no runway below, and he had lost his radio, compass and fuel gauge in the storm.
The black aeroplane appeared beside him, guided him through the clouds and then vanished before he landed.
The Paris control room reported that the radar showed an unidentified plane flying beside him the whole time.
These details suggest the helper was not an ordinary pilot — it reads like the pilot's own courage, or a guardian spirit, and the story leaves the question deliberately open.

qa.q: 'Both the stories are about overcoming fear.' Justify with reference to the two stories.
a: In **His First Flight**, the young seagull is paralysed by fear while his brothers and sister fly. His parents scold him and his siblings taunt him, but fear keeps him on the ledge for twenty-four hours. Only extreme hunger, and the sight of his mother with a piece of fish, drive him to dive — and in that desperate moment he discovers that his wings do support him. His fear is overcome by necessity and by the example of his family.

In **The Black Aeroplane**, the narrator is an experienced pilot, but the storm terrifies him: the compass and radio fail, he cannot see anything, and he has only a few minutes of fuel left. His fear is overcome by following the mysterious black aeroplane, whose pilot leads him out of the storm and vanishes. He never finds out who helped him, which suggests that the courage came from within.
In both stories, fear is conquered only by taking the leap — the seagull by diving, the pilot by following into the dark — and in both the reward is a safe arrival.

qa.q: Draw a character sketch of the young seagull and show how he changes from the beginning of the story to the end.
a: At first he is timid and afraid: he stays on the ledge while his brothers and sisters fly.
He is stubborn in his fear: he ignores the coaxing and scolding of his family.
He is also very hungry, and this makes him forget his fear for a moment and dive for the fish.
Once in the air he finds that his wings carry him; he becomes joyful and confident.
The change shows that fear is often only in the mind, and that an experience can end it.

mcq.q: 'His First Flight' is written by: (a) Frederick Forsyth (b) Liam O'Flaherty (c) G. L. Fuentes (d) Gavin Maxwell
mcq.a: **(b) Liam O'Flaherty.**

mcq.q: How long was the young seagull left alone on his ledge before he flew? (a) twelve hours (b) twenty-four hours (c) two days (d) three days
mcq.a: **(b) twenty-four hours**, during which he was hungry and afraid while his siblings flew.

mcq.q: In 'The Black Aeroplane', the woman in the control centre told the narrator that: (a) the other pilot had landed elsewhere (b) there was no other aeroplane in the sky that night (c) the black plane was a military aircraft (d) the radar had failed
mcq.a: **(b) there was no other aeroplane in the sky that night**, and no other plane on the radar.

mcq.q: “The Black Aeroplane” was written by: (a) Liam O’Flaherty (b) Anton Chekhov (c) Frederick Forsyth (d) Gavin Maxwell
mcq.a: **(c) Frederick Forsyth.** Frederick Forsyth wrote The Black Aeroplane; Liam O’Flaherty wrote His First Flight.

mcq.q: The young seagull finally flew when he: (a) was pushed off the ledge by his father (b) saw a storm approaching (c) followed another bird over the sea (d) dived at the piece of fish his mother held
mcq.a: **(d) dived at the piece of fish his mother held.** Hunger overcame his fear, and in diving for the fish he found that he could fly.

mcq.q: In ‘His First Flight', the young seagull's mother tempted him with: (a) a piece of fish  (b) a worm  (c) a leaf  (d) her call alone
mcq.a: **(a) a piece of fish.** Hunger overcame his fear and he dived for it.

mcq.q: The narrator of ‘The Black Aeroplane' was flying his Dakota from: (a) London to Paris  (b) Paris to London  (c) New York to Paris  (d) Dakar to Paris
mcq.a: **(b) Paris to London.** He wanted to reach England for breakfast with his family.

mcq.q: The young seagull was afraid to fly because: (a) he hated his family (b) he felt his wings would not support him over the great depth below (c) he was ill (d) the weather was bad
mcq.a: **(b) he felt his wings would not support him over the great depth below.** Fear of falling kept him on the ledge for twenty-four hours.

onepager: - His First Flight: O'Flaherty; 24 hours on the ledge; hunger and the sight of fish break the fear.
- The Black Aeroplane: Forsyth; storm over France; instruments fail; a black plane with no lights leads him out.
- The control centre says no other plane was in the sky.
- Common theme: fear is conquered only by taking the leap.
task: Retell each story in five sentences, then write one sentence stating the common theme. In the exam you may be asked for either story at short notice, and this drill makes both available in under two minutes.
steps: 1. Say which of the **two stories** you are answering — 'His First Flight' or 'The Black Aeroplane'.
2. For the young seagull: the fear, the hunger, the desperate dive, and the parents circling with scraps of dogfish.
3. For the pilot: the storm, the lost compass and radio, and the **black aeroplane** that guides him to safety.
4. Close on the **theme** — the first flight is the first act of independence, and the second story leaves the question of who helped deliberately open.

title: From the Diary of Anne Frank
short: A thirteen-year-old's first diary entries and her punishment essay.
lede: Anne Frank's own words. Two essays and one teacher are the whole plot — but the voice is what is examined.
lens: Reference-to-context extracts, usually from the opening passage about why she keeps a diary, or from the essay 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox'.
Know why she began the diary, why she needed a friend, and what Mr Keesing asked her to write about.
concepts: **1. Summary.** Thirteen-year-old Anne Frank begins her diary, which she names **Kitty**, on her thirteenth birthday. She explains that **'paper has more patience than people'**: she has a loving family, an adoring father and mother, a sixteen-year-old sister Margot, about thirty friends and many admirers, but no **true friend** to whom she can confide her innermost thoughts. Her grandmother, whom she loved very much, died in January 1942; Anne's entry of June 1942 is followed by her family going into hiding in July. She is a student in a Jewish secondary school in Amsterdam.

**2. The essays.** Her mathematics teacher, **Mr Keesing**, is annoyed by her talking in class and assigns her an essay titled **'A Chatterbox'**. Anne writes three pages and argues that talking is a student's trait and that she would try to keep it under control, but that she would never be able to cure herself of the habit since her mother talks as much as she does — and there is little one can do about inherited traits. Mr Keesing takes the joke in the right spirit. The next time she talks he assigns **'An Incorrigible Chatterbox'**. The third time he sets **'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox'** as punishment, this time to be written in verse. Anne's friend **Sanne** helps, and Anne writes the poem about a mother duck and a father swan whose three ducklings are bitten to death because they quacked too much. Mr Keesing reads it to his own class and to another class, adds his own comments, and from then on allows Anne to talk in class and never gives her any extra homework. To Anne he is **'the nicest teacher'** she has ever met.

**3. Themes.** The **need for a friend and for a private voice**; **the gap between the self one shows and the self one feels**; **humour as a defence**; and the shadow of the **Jewish experience under Nazi rule**, which the diary entries only hint at.
tricks: - **'Paper has more patience than people'** — the single most quoted line from this chapter; learn it exactly.
- **Three essays in order:** A Chatterbox → An Incorrigible Chatterbox → Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox.
- Anne argues her talking is an **inherited trait** from her mother — that argument is what wins Mr Keesing over.
mistakes: - Saying Anne had no friends at all. She had about thirty friends and admirers, but **no true friend** to confide in.
- Naming the diary 'Anne'. She named it **Kitty**.
- Describing Mr Keesing as strict and unkind throughout. He turns out to be, in Anne's words, **the nicest teacher**.

qa.q: Why did Anne Frank feel the need for a diary?
qa.a: Because although she had a loving family, friends and admirers, she had no true friend — nobody to whom she could confide her innermost thoughts. She wrote that paper has more patience than people, so she began the diary as a substitute for a real friend, and named it Kitty.

qa.q: What argument did Anne make in her first essay, 'A Chatterbox'?
qa.a: She argued that talking is a student's trait and that she would try to keep it under control, but that she would never be able to cure herself completely of the habit, because her mother talks as much as she does. She added that there is little one can do about inherited traits — an argument which Mr Keesing took in the right spirit.

qa.q: What does Anne write about her grandmother?
qa.a: Anne writes that nobody knows how often she thinks of her grandmother and still loves her. Her grandmother was born in 1888 and died in January 1942, and Anne says that she wrote the diary partly so that this love would not be lost. She adds that this whole diary was written in the thought of her grandmother.

qa.q: A student writes that Anne had no friends and named her diary “Anne”. Correct both statements.
a: Anne had many friends and admirers, about thirty of them, but no **true** friend with whom she could share her deepest thoughts.
She named her diary **Kitty** and wrote to it as to a friend.
She felt that “paper has more patience than people”, so she could pour out her feelings in it.

qa.q: Many teenagers today keep a diary or a blog. Compare their reasons with Anne’s and give two similarities.
a: Like Anne, they want a private place to express feelings they cannot share easily with others.
They also use writing to understand themselves and to record events and memories.
A difference is that Anne wrote in hiding and for herself, while a blog today is often written for an audience.

qa.q: Why did Anne Frank decide to keep a diary?
a: She had no real friend in whom she could confide; although she had many acquaintances, she could not discuss her innermost thoughts with them.
A diary cannot talk back, and she felt that paper has more patience than people.
She wanted to write out her deepest thoughts and feelings, and the diary became the friend she called Kitty.

qa.q: What was Anne's argument in her third essay, and why did it win over Mr Keesing?
a: The third essay was a poem — ‘Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox’ — about a mother duck and a father swan whose three ducklings are bitten to death by the father for quacking too much.

The joke was aimed at Mr Keesing himself: too much punishment for too much talking. Luckily he took it the right way, laughed, read it to the class, and from then on let Anne talk — becoming, in her words, the nicest teacher.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Anne writes, “Paper has more patience than people.”

(a) Which figure of speech is used?
(b) What does the sentence mean?
(c) How does it explain why Anne began a diary?
a: (a) Personification (paper is given the human quality of patience); it is also a comparison.
(b) A page will listen without interrupting or judging, but people often do not have the time or patience to listen.
(c) She had no friend who would listen in that way, so she chose to write instead.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Anne says that she has many friends and admirers, but that when she is with them, “we just can’t seem to get any closer”.

(a) What does she mean by a true friend?
(b) Why can she not share her feelings with her acquaintances?
(c) What does she hope the diary will be?
a: (a) Someone to whom she could confide her innermost thoughts.
(b) With them she talks only about ordinary things and the talk never becomes deeper.
(c) A friend, whom she calls Kitty, who will listen with “patience”.

qa.q: Describe Mr Keesing's punishment and how Anne used it to her advantage.
a: Anne was caught talking in class, so the maths teacher Mr Keesing gave her extra homework: first an essay on ‘A Chatterbox', then ‘An Incorrigible Chatterbox', and then ‘Quack Quack Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox'.
Anne wrote the first essay arguing that talking is a student's trait which she inherited from her mother and could never cure.
For the second she argued that she could not stop talking in a maths class because it was impossible to keep quiet.
For the third she wrote a poem about a swan with three ducklings that bit their father to death, and illustrated it; Mr Keesing was amused, read the poem to the class and stopped punishing her.

qa.q: Describe Mr Keesing and how his attitude towards Anne changed.
a: **Mr Keesing** was Anne's mathematics teacher, an old-fashioned teacher who was annoyed by her constant talking in class. He punished her by assigning an essay titled 'A Chatterbox'.

**Anne's response:** she wrote three pages, admitting the habit but arguing that talking is a student's trait and that her mother talks as much as she does, so it is an inherited trait and there is little one can do about it. Mr Keesing took the joke in the right spirit.

**The second and third essays:** when she talked again he assigned 'An Incorrigible Chatterbox', and the third time he set 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox' — this time in verse. With the help of her friend Sanne, Anne wrote a comic poem about a mother duck and a father swan whose three ducklings are bitten to death by the swan for quacking too much.

**The change:** Mr Keesing read the poem to his own class and then to another class, adding his own comments, and laughed at it. From then on he allowed Anne to talk in class and never gave her extra homework again. Anne calls him the nicest teacher she ever met.

qa.q: What picture of Anne’s personality emerges from the extract? Support your answer with four qualities.
a: Talkative and cheerful: she is called a chatterbox and cannot stop talking in class.
Witty and creative: she turns a punishment into a poem and makes the teacher laugh.
Honest: she admits her failing and does not pretend to be different.
Affectionate and thoughtful: she writes lovingly about her grandmother and longs for a true friend.
Together they show a lively, perceptive girl who uses writing to make sense of life.

mcq.q: Anne named her diary: (a) Margot (b) Kitty (c) Sanne (d) Anne
mcq.a: **(b) Kitty** — she treated the diary as the true friend she did not have.

mcq.q: The third essay Mr Keesing assigned was: (a) A Chatterbox (b) An Incorrigible Chatterbox (c) Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox (d) A Talkative Girl
mcq.a: **(c) Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox**, and this time it had to be written in verse.

mcq.q: The line 'paper has more patience than people' means that: (a) paper lasts longer than people (b) a diary will listen without judging or tiring (c) people are impatient with writing (d) diaries are more valuable than friends
mcq.a: **(b)** — Anne could write things to paper that she could never say aloud to a person.

mcq.q: Anne Frank named her diary: (a) Kitty (b) Anne (c) Margot (d) Peter
mcq.a: **(a) Kitty.** She addressed her diary as Kitty, the friend she did not have.

mcq.q: The title of Anne’s third essay for Mr Keesing was: (a) “Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox” (b) “A Chatterbox” (c) “An Incorrigible Chatterbox” (d) “My Grandmother”
mcq.a: **(a) “Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox”.** The third essay was a humorous poem about a mother duck and her ducklings, which won Mr Keesing over.

mcq.q: Anne Frank named her diary: (a) Kitty  (b) Margot  (c) Lies  (d) Sanne
mcq.a: **(a) Kitty.** She addressed all her entries to this imaginary friend.

mcq.q: Anne and her family went into hiding in: (a) Amsterdam  (b) Berlin  (c) Paris  (d) Frankfurt
mcq.a: **(a) Amsterdam.** They hid in the secret annexe behind her father's office on the Prinsengracht.

mcq.q: Anne's grandmother died in: (a) January 1942 (b) July 1942 (c) June 1941 (d) December 1942
mcq.a: **(a) January 1942.** Anne writes that no one could understand her serious illness, and her birthday candles were lit in her memory.

trend: The reason Anne began the diary and Mr Keesing's three essays alternate as the set questions; the 'paper has more patience than people' line recurs as a short extract.
onepager: - Anne, 13, Amsterdam; family goes into hiding in July 1942; grandmother died January 1942.
- No true friend, so the diary 'Kitty' replaces one; 'paper has more patience than people'.
- Three essays: A Chatterbox → An Incorrigible Chatterbox → Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox.
- Mr Keesing becomes 'the nicest teacher' after reading the poem.
task: Write a one-page diary entry of your own in Anne's voice — starting with why you are writing it, as she does. The exercise forces you to notice that her opening is an argument, not an introduction, which is exactly what the extract question tests.
steps: 1. Set the **situation**: the Frank family in hiding in the Secret Annexe, and Anne writing to 'Kitty'.
2. Explain why a thirteen-year-old wants a **true friend** and a diary — she cannot pour her heart out to the people she lives with.
3. Describe the **classroom incident** — the talkativeness, the essays, the essay 'Quack, Quack, Quack, said Mistress Chatterbox'.
4. End with what the diary proves: **paper has more patience than people**, and Anne's humour survives the hiding.

title: Glimpses of India
short: Goa's bakers, Assam's tea country and Coorg's people.
lede: Three short travel pieces in one chapter. Each is examined separately, so treat them as three mini-chapters.
lens: Extracts and short answers are set from any one of the three parts; the question usually names the part.
**A Baker from Goa** — Lucio Rodrigues. **Coorg** — Lokesh Abrol. **Tea from Assam** — Arup Kumar Datta.
concepts: **1. A Baker from Goa (Lucio Rodrigues).** In the old days of Portuguese rule, bakers — known as **pader** — were an important part of Goan life. Their arrival was announced by the **'jang, jhang, jhang'** of the bamboo staff they carried, one hand on the basket of loaves and the other banging the staff on the ground. Children ran to meet them, not for the bread (which the maid-servant bought) but to choose the **bread bangles**, or sometimes the sweet specially-made loaves. The baker always came twice a day — once early in the morning and again when he returned after emptying his basket. Baking was a **profitable profession**; the baker and his family never starved, and they always looked **fat and jolly** — even today, anyone with a jackfruit-like physique is compared to a baker. Bread is essential: **bol** (sweet bread) for marriage gifts, **bolinhas** and coconut cookies for Christmas, sandwiches for a daughter's engagement, and **pao** for the feast. The baker wore a peculiar dress, the **kabai**, a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees; in the writer's childhood the bakers wore a shirt and trousers shorter than full-length ones. Monthly accounts were recorded on the wall in pencil, and the furnaces still exist.

**2. Coorg (Lokesh Abrol).** Coorg, or **Kodagu**, is the smallest district of Karnataka, midway between Mysore and the coastal town of Mangalore — a piece of heaven that must have drifted from the kingdom of god. It is a rolling hillside with a permanent fragrance of coffee, coffee estates and spice plantations, colonial bungalows under treetops, and forests. The season of joy is from **September to March**. The people of Coorg are a **proud race of martial men, beautiful women and wild creatures**; a popular theory traces their descent to **Alexander's army**, which moved south along the coast and settled there, marrying among the locals. Another theory claims **Arab origin**, since the **Kuppia**, the long black coat with an embroidered waist-belt worn by the Kodavus, resembles the **kuffia** worn by the Arabs and the Kurds. Coorgis are the **most hospitable people in India**, and are the only people in India permitted to carry firearms without a licence. The **Kaveri river** originates from the hills and forests of Coorg; **Mahaseer**, a large freshwater fish, is found there, and kingfishers, squirrels, langurs and wild elephants can be seen. The climb to the **Brahmagiri hills** gives a view of the whole misty landscape of Coorg, and a walk to the sixty-acre **Buddhist monastery** at **Bylakuppe** is a surprise.

**3. Tea from Assam (Arup Kumar Datta).** Rajvir, a boy from Assam, travels to Delhi with Pranjol, whose father manages the **Dhekiajuli Tea Estate**. On the way they stop at a tea stall, where Rajvir hears that **eighty crore cups of tea are drunk every day throughout the world**. Pranjol's father meets them at Mariani junction and drives them through the **Dhekiajuli** estate, where acres of neatly pruned bushes stretch to the horizon with shade trees. Pranjol's mother welcomes them with tea and snacks. In the garden, the workers with bamboo baskets on their backs pluck the newly sprouted leaves. Pranjol's mother says that the Chinese legend says tea was first drunk in China around **2700 BC**, when some leaves from a burning twig fell into boiling water and gave a delicious drink; **Marco Polo** and **Bodhidharma** are also linked to tea legends. The second-sprouting period, from **May to July**, yields the finest tea. Tea was first brought to India from China by the British, and India now produces some of the finest tea in the world.
tricks: - **Pader, kabai, bol, bolinhas, pao** — five Goan words that anchor the Goa extract.
- **Coorg = coffee fragrance + martial men + firearms without licence + Kuppia coat.** Four markers, one paragraph.
- **Eighty crore cups a day** is the number asked most often in the Assam extract.
mistakes: - Saying Coorg is in Kerala. It is **Kodavu, in Karnataka**, the smallest district, between Mysore and Mangalore.
- Confusing **bol** (sweet bread for marriage gifts) with **bolinhas** (coconut cookies for Christmas).
- Giving the tea date as 2700 AD. The Chinese legend places it around **2700 BC**.

qa.q: Why is the baker called a friend, companion and guide in Goa?
qa.a: Because he was woven into the daily life of the village. His arrival, announced by the jangling of his bamboo staff, was a fixed event twice a day, and children ran to meet him to choose their bread bangles. He was present at every celebration — bol for marriages, bolinhas and coconut cookies for Christmas, sandwiches for engagements — so his presence marked the family's important occasions.

qa.q: What do you know about the people of Coorg?
qa.a: They are a proud race of martial men, beautiful women and wild creatures. They are perhaps the most hospitable people in India and are the only people in India permitted to carry firearms without a licence. One theory says they are descended from a part of Alexander's army that settled there and married among the locals; another says they are of Arab origin, because the Kuppia, the long black coat with an embroidered waist-belt worn by the Kodavus, resembles the kuffia worn by Arabs and Kurds.

qa.q: How does the legend of tea connect China and India?
qa.a: According to a Chinese legend, tea was first drunk in China around 2700 BC, when a few leaves from a twig burning under a vessel of boiling water fell into it and gave a delicious drink. An Indian legend says that Bodhidharma, an ancient Buddhist ascetic, cut off his eyelids because he felt sleepy during meditation, and ten tea plants grew out of the eyelids; the leaves of these plants, when put in hot water and drunk, banished sleep. Tea came to Europe only in the sixteenth century, and was drunk more as medicine than as a beverage.

qa.q: A student writes that Coorg is in Kerala and that the Chinese legend of tea goes back to 2700 AD. Correct both statements.
a: Coorg (Kodagu) is in **Karnataka**; it is the smallest district of the state and lies midway between Mysore and Mangalore.
According to the Chinese legend, tea was first drunk around **2700 BC**, when leaves from a burning twig fell into a vessel of boiling water.
(An Indian legend adds that tea plants grew from the eyelids of the monk Bodhidharma.)

qa.q: The Goan baker is part of village life. Name one person from your own locality, such as a milkman or a postman, who is similarly part of community life, and explain how in about three lines.
a: Any suitable example, for instance the milkman who comes every morning.
He is part of daily routine: people know the sound or time of his arrival and plan around it.
Like the baker, he is present in families’ regular life and sometimes in special occasions, so people think of him as a friend and not only a seller.

qa.q: What is a ‘pader' and how does Goa's Portuguese inheritance survive in its bread?
a: A pader is the traditional Goan baker; the descendants of these bakers still run the bread business in Goa.
The Portuguese introduced the leavened bread called pao, which is still the staple of every Goan meal alongside rice, fish, curry and vegetables.
The bread is baked in the old-fashioned ‘pod' or mud ovens, and the baker's bamboo staff thumping on the floor is still heard at dawn.
Marriage gifts called ‘bol' and the sweet bread of special occasions keep the tradition alive.

qa.q: The chapter covers Goa, Coorg and Assam. What does each place contribute to the ‘glimpse of India’?
a: Goa contributes living history — the Portuguese pader, the kabai and the bol show how a colonial past survives in daily bread.
Coorg contributes landscape and valour — coffee-scented hills, the martial Kodavus and the Kaveri's origin.
Assam contributes a global story — tea drunk eighty crore cups a day, linking Chinese legend and Indian gardens. Together they show India's variety.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

In Goa, the baker announces himself with the jingling of his bamboo staff, and the children rush to him to pick their bread bangles.

(a) What announces the baker’s arrival?
(b) Name the breads or cookies made for a wedding and for Christmas.
(c) What does the baker’s role show about Goan culture?
a: (a) The jingling of the bamboo staff that he thumps on the floor.
(b) *Bol* is the sweet bread made for marriages and *bolinhas* are the coconut cookies of Christmas.
(c) The Portuguese influence lives on in food, and the baker marks every important family occasion.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

The Kodavus of Coorg are described as a proud, martial race.

(a) What special privilege do they have?
(b) What two theories are given about their origin?
(c) What clue supports the Arab theory?
a: (a) They are the only people in India allowed to carry firearms without a licence.
(b) That they descended from part of Alexander’s army that settled in Coorg, or that they are of Arab origin.
(c) Their traditional long black coat with an embroidered waist-belt, the *kuppia*, resembles the *kuffia* worn by Arabs and Kurds.

qa.q: Describe Rajvir's journey to Assam and what he saw in the tea gardens.
a: Rajvir travelled by train to Dhekiabari with his friend Pranjol, whose father managed a tea estate.
As the train neared the tea country, Rajvir looked out at endless stretches of orderly tea bushes and doll-like women plucking leaves.
Pranjol, who had grown up on a plantation, slept through it, but Rajvir could not sleep with excitement.

He impressed Pranjol with his knowledge: the second flush or sprouting period gives the best tea, and he told the legend of the Chinese emperor who discovered tea when leaves fell into his boiling water.

qa.q: Describe the Coorg landscape and its attractions.
a: Coorg, or Kodagu, is the smallest district of Karnataka, lying midway between Mysore and the coastal town of Mangalore. It is a rolling hillside with a permanent fragrance of fresh coffee, coffee estates and spice plantations, colonial bungalows tucked under treetops, and dense forests.
**The best season** is from September to March, when the weather is perfect, the air breathes of invigorating coffee, and the rain showers keep the hills fresh.

**Wildlife:** the Kaveri river, which takes its birth from the hills and forests of Coorg, is home to Mahaseer, a large freshwater fish; kingfishers, squirrels and langurs can be seen, and wild elephants bathe in the river.

**Attractions:** the climb to the Brahmagiri hills gives a panoramic view of the entire misty landscape of Coorg; a walk into the sixty-acre Buddhist monastery at Bylakutte, hidden among the coffee plantations, is a surprise; and there are rappelling, river rafting, canoeing and rock climbing for the adventurous.

title: Mijbil the Otter
short: Gavin Maxwell, an otter named Mijbil, and a journey to London.
lede: A true account of keeping an otter as a pet. The details — the water, the suitcase, the plane — are what is asked.
lens: Reference-to-context extracts and a long answer on Maxwell's feelings towards Mijbil or on the otter's habits.
Know where Maxwell was (Basra, Iraq), why he wanted an otter, what Mijbil did on the aeroplane, and what the Londoners thought he was.
concepts: **1. Summary.** In **1956** the author, **Gavin Maxwell**, travelled to **Basra in Iraq** to the Consulate-General to collect and answer his mail from Europe. His pet otter had died, and his friend suggested he get an **otter from the Tigris marshes**. Two Arabs brought him a small otter in a sack — a creature he had never seen before, resembling most of all a small, medievally-conceived dragon. He named it **Mijbil**, and scientists later classified it as a previously unrecognised species, *Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli*, or **Maxwell's otter**. Mijbil spent most of his time playing in the bathroom water, plunging and rolling in it, and shuffling on the tiled floor. When they went to **London**, Mijbil escaped from the box on the aeroplane, ran along the aircraft, and tore the lining to shreds, so Maxwell had to catch him — Mijbil came and sat on his knee and nuzzled his face. In London, Mijbil invented games with **marbles, ping-pong balls and rubber fruit**, and would play with them for hours. He learned to walk on a lead and developed compulsive habits, such as jumping over a low wall and running along the boundary wall of a school, where the children made noise. Londoners, who had never seen an otter, guessed that it was **'a baby seal', 'a squirrel', 'a walrus', 'a hippo', 'a beaver', 'a bear cub', 'a leopard'** or even **'a brontosaurus'**. Maxwell reflects that Mijbil seemed to have certain characteristics: he was, like a child, both **restless and full of joy**, and he had a strong need for the company and affection of human beings.

**2. Mijbil's intelligence and mischief.** Mijbil learns the bathroom taps, opens the door, and turns every pool of water into a game — he 'would juggle with a rubber ball' and keep it spinning on his nose. His curiosity is never still: he disappears into the wall, chews the wallpaper, and once leaves blood on the floor that sends Maxwell into a panic, only for the blood to turn out to be from a fish he had found. These episodes are the answer to every question about the otter's **nature**.

**3. The journey and the bond.** Travel to England means a box, airline rules, and a crate — yet Mijbil chooses to stay with Maxwell rather than run to the open marshes. On the flight he escapes the box once the door is opened, and Maxwell only has to call his name for the otter to come back to him. **Obedience born of affection, not training** — that is the point of the ending, and the sentence that closes most full-mark answers.
tricks: - **Water is everything:** Mijbil's joy was plunging and rolling in water — 'he would screw the tap up and then play in the trickle'.
- The London guesses list is a favourite 1-mark MCQ: seal, squirrel, walrus, hippo, beaver, bear cub, leopard, brontosaurus.
- Maxwell's own conclusion: Mijbil was **like a child** — restless, joyful and needing company.
mistakes: - Saying Maxwell found Mijbil in the wild himself. Two **Arabs** brought him the otter in a sack.
- Placing the story in Kerala, because of the Tigris marshes confusion. It begins in **Basra, Iraq**.
- Forgetting that the species was named after Maxwell — *Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli*.

qa.q: What things does Mijbil do which tell you that he is an intelligent, friendly and fun-loving animal who needs love?
qa.a: He invented games with marbles, ping-pong balls and rubber fruit, and could keep himself amused for hours. He learned to walk on a lead and to respond to his name. He escaped from his box on the aeroplane, but instead of running away he came back and sat on Maxwell's knee and nuzzled his face — showing affection rather than fear. He developed compulsive rituals of his own, like the wall-jumping routine he repeated every day on the way to school, which shows both intelligence and a need for company.

qa.q: Why did Maxwell think the air-hostess was 'the very queen of her kind'?
qa.a: Because when he told her about Mijbil and the trouble he expected on the flight, she was extremely friendly and helpful. She suggested that he keep the box on his knee, and her kindness made a difficult journey possible — so he called her the very queen of her kind.

qa.q: What guesses did the Londoners make about what Mijbil was?
qa.a: A Londoner who had never seen an otter made wild guesses: that it was a baby seal, a squirrel, a walrus, a hippo, a beaver, a bear cub, a leopard — one even said it was a brontosaurus. None of them recognised the animal, because otters were unknown in London.

qa.q: A student writes that Maxwell caught Mijbil himself in the wild and that the story begins in Kerala. Correct both statements.
a: Two Arabs brought Maxwell the otter from the Tigris marshes; he did not catch it himself.
The story begins at **Basra, in Iraq**, where Maxwell decided to keep the otter and named it Mijbil.
Later, zoologists found it to be a new subspecies, which was named after Maxwell.

qa.q: Maxwell took many precautions when he travelled with Mijbil. What do they show about him?
a: He packed Mijbil in a box that met the airline’s size limit and lined it so that it was secure.
He told the air-hostess in advance and kept the box close to him, so he thought about the animal’s safety.
So he is responsible, resourceful and kind to animals; he cared for Mijbil as a companion, not a curiosity.

qa.q: How did Mijbil behave during the flight to London?
a: At first he was upset and kept trying to escape, rolling and twisting in his box.
Once Maxwell let him out, he disappeared onto the aircraft and scrambled over luggage, seats and passengers, creating chaos for a quarter of an hour.
Maxwell caught him by the tail and returned him to the box, and thereafter the otter slept.
On the drive home Mijbil again escaped and was finally found on the floor of the car under the driver's seat.

qa.q: How did Maxwell get Mijbil, and why was the otter's species named after him?
a: In 1956, at Basra in Iraq, two Arabs brought Maxwell an otter from the Tigris marshes; he named it Mijbil and decided to keep it.
When zoologists examined it, they found it belonged to a previously unknown subspecies, which they named Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli — after Maxwell himself.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Mijbil put a terrapin into his box, shut the lid and pushed the box across the floor, using it as a sledge down slopes and into the water.

(a) What does this game show about Mijbil?
(b) Name two other things he played with.
(c) What does it show about Maxwell?
a: (a) That he is intelligent, curious and inventive, and loves play.
(b) A rubber ball, marbles or ping-pong balls.
(c) That he watched Mijbil closely and with affection, and gave him company and occupation.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

The airline insisted that Mijbil be packed in a box no more than eighteen inches square. Soon after take-off, he tore its lining and escaped.

(a) Where was the box to be kept during the flight?
(b) What happened after Mijbil escaped?
(c) How did Maxwell finally catch him?
a: (a) On the floor, near Maxwell’s feet.
(b) He ran down the aircraft and scrambled over luggage, seats and passengers, and a girl screamed “A rat!”.
(c) Maxwell caught him by the tail and put him back in the box, after which the otter slept.

qa.q: What games did Mijbil invent, and what do they show about him?
a: He invented a game with a terrapin: he put the terrapin in his box and shut the lid, then pushed the box around the floor and used it as a sledge down slopes and into the water.
He also played with a rubber ball, which he kept dipping into water and rolling, and with marbles rattling along the corrugated surface of a suitcase.
The games show an animal of unusual intelligence and curiosity, who needs company and occupation and who learns by playing.
They also show how closely Maxwell observed him, and why the otter stayed devoted to him.

qa.q: Describe the journey from Basra to London and the trouble Mijbil caused on the aeroplane.
a: Maxwell had to travel to London with Mijbil, and the airline insisted that the otter be packed in a box not more than eighteen inches square, to be carried on the floor near his feet.

Thirty minutes before the flight, the box was lined with metal and Mijbil was put inside. When the plane took off, Mijbil tore the lining to shreds and escaped. He ran at high speed down the aircraft, and passengers cried out; a girl screamed 'A rat! A rat!'

Maxwell dived across the legs of other passengers to catch him, but Mijbil disappeared. When he returned to his seat he found the air-hostess with the otter on her knee. She had caught him and held him.
Mijbil then came back to Maxwell, sat on his knee and began to nuzzle his face and his neck, so the journey ended with the otter calm again, though the box was in tatters.

qa.q: What does “Mijbil the Otter” tell us about the relationship between humans and wild animals?
a: Maxwell’s bond with Mijbil began with curiosity but grew into real affection and responsibility.
He learned the animal’s needs by careful observation, for example his love of water and play.
The animal responded with trust: after escaping on the plane, Mijbil came back and sat on Maxwell’s knee.
The story also shows that a wild animal needs space, occupation and company, which a pet owner must provide.
It leaves the reader respecting the animal and its natural habits, not treating it as a toy.

mcq.q: Mijbil was scientifically classified as: (a) Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli (b) Lutra lutra (c) Aonyx cinereus (d) Enhydra lutris
mcq.a: **(a) Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli** — a previously unrecognised species, named Maxwell's otter after Gavin Maxwell.

mcq.q: Where did the author collect Mijbil from? (a) Kerala (b) the Tigris marshes near Basra (c) the Nile delta (d) Assam
mcq.a: **(b) the Tigris marshes near Basra in Iraq**, where two Arabs brought him the otter in a sack.

mcq.q: On the aeroplane Mijbil: (a) slept throughout (b) escaped from his box and tore the lining to shreds (c) bit the air-hostess (d) refused to eat
mcq.a: **(b)** — he escaped, ran down the aircraft and tore the box lining; later he returned to sit on Maxwell's knee.

mcq.q: Mijbil was brought to Maxwell at: (a) London in England (b) Basra in Iraq (c) Kochi in Kerala (d) Cairo in Egypt
mcq.a: **(b) Basra in Iraq.** The otter came from the Tigris marshes and was handed to Maxwell at Basra.

mcq.q: The subspecies of otter that Maxwell’s Mijbil belonged to was named: (a) Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli (b) Lutra lutra mijbili (c) Aonyx cinerea basrae (d) Enhydra lutris maxwelli
mcq.a: **(a) Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli.** Zoologists named the new subspecies after Maxwell, who had brought it to light.

mcq.q: Mijbil was an otter of the species found in: (a) the marshes of southern Iraq  (b) the Amazon  (c) the Himalayas  (d) Africa
mcq.a: **(a) the marshes of southern Iraq.** Maxwell named him Mijbil and trained him to obey a lead.

mcq.q: The author of ‘Mijbil the Otter' is: (a) Gavin Maxwell  (b) Gerald Durrell  (c) Ruskin Bond  (d) James Herriot
mcq.a: **(a) Gavin Maxwell.** The extract is from his book *Ring of Bright Water*.

mcq.q: Mijbil loved to play with: (a) marbles and ping-pong balls (b) sticks and stones (c) paper boats (d) balloons
mcq.a: **(a) marbles and ping-pong balls.** He juggled them lying on his back and invented compulsive games with them.

trend: The aeroplane episode and the Londoners' guesses alternate as the set extract; Mijbil's play with water and marbles is the recurring 3-mark answer.
onepager: - 1956, Basra; two Arabs bring the otter; named Mijbil; species named after Maxwell.
- Loves water, marbles, ping-pong balls and rubber fruit; develops compulsive daily rituals.
- Escapes on the plane, tears the lining, returns to nuzzle Maxwell.
