task: List six things Mijbil does that show intelligence and six that show affection, in two columns. Then write one sentence linking both to Maxwell's conclusion that he was like a child — that single sentence is worth two marks in the exam.
steps: 1. Open with the **setting and the loss** — Basra, 1956, the Consulate-General, and the otter that had died before Mijbil arrived.
2. Describe Mijbil's arrival in the sack and Maxwell's reaction — 'a small, medievally-conceived dragon', later identified as *Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli*.
3. Give **two incidents** that show his intelligence and mischief: the water games in the bathroom, and the blood on the floor that turned out to be a fish.
4. Close with the **bond** — Mijbil follows Maxwell like a dog, and the journey to England that proves otters attach themselves to people, not places.

title: Madam Rides the Bus
short: Valliammai's eight-year-old journey, and what she learns on the way back.
lede: A child's independence and her first meeting with death — in one bus ride.
lens: Extracts from the planning of the journey, or from the return trip when Valli sees the dead cow.
Know her age (**eight years and some months**), the fare (**thirty paise each way**), the journey time (**forty-five minutes**), and what she refused on the bus.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Valliammai**, called **Valli** for short, was an eight-year-old girl — eight years and some months — who lived in a village. Her favourite pastime was standing in the **front doorway of her house** and watching what was happening in the street outside, because there were no other children of her own age. The sight that filled her with **unbelievable desire** was the bus that travelled between her village and the nearest town. It was a new bus, painted a gleaming white, with silver overhead bars; when it started, it seemed to be coming towards them, then turned and went back to the town. Day after day she watched it, and she gathered details by listening to conversations: the town was **six miles** away, the fare was **thirty paise one way**, and the trip took **forty-five minutes**. She saved the money by resisting every temptation to buy peppermints, toys and balloons, and by staying away from the merry-go-round at the village fair.

**2. The journey.** Valli stood up on her seat so that she could see everything: the bus ran along the bank of a canal, past palm trees, grassland, distant mountains and a blue sky. She saw a **young cow** running in front of the bus; the driver sounded the horn again and again, and the cow turned and looked at them and then ran faster, which made Valli laugh until tears filled her eyes. At the town, the conductor offered her a cold drink, but she refused and asked only to be taken back on the same bus. He called her **'madam'** throughout, and she insisted on being treated as an adult.

**3. The return.** On the way back, Valli saw the **same young cow lying dead by the roadside**, with her legs spread out, eyes lifeless and a fixed stare, and blood all over. She was horrified and had no desire to laugh any more. She did not want to look out of the window and sat glued to her seat. She reached her village at about **1:45 p.m.**, and found her mother awake and talking to an aunt. When her aunt asked where she had been, Valli's mother said she had been sleeping and had gone nowhere; Valli smiled to herself, because she had been so many places — and all without anyone knowing.

**4. Themes.** **Growing up and independence** — a child who plans and executes a journey alone. **Curiosity** — learning by listening and observing. **The first encounter with death** — the dead cow changes her, and the loss of innocence is the point of the ending.
tricks: - **Thirty paise each way, six miles, forty-five minutes.** Those three numbers are the most common 1-mark items.
- The **cow appears twice** — alive on the way out, dead on the way back. That contrast is the whole point of the story.
- The conductor calls her **'madam'** — hence the title.
mistakes: - Saying Valli took the bus with her mother. She went **alone**; that is the point.
- Giving her age as eight years. It is **eight years and some months**, which she is proud of.
- Missing the ending: Valli does not tell anyone, and her mother still thinks she was asleep.

qa.q: Why was the bus journey such a fascination for Valli?
qa.a: Because she had never been to the town and had no companions of her own age, so the bus became her window on the world. Every day it passed her house twice, carrying new people each time, and she longed to travel on it. The sight of the gleaming white bus, with its silver overhead bars and the people inside, filled her with an unbelievable desire, and the thought of travelling to the town and back grew stronger and stronger until she saved enough money to do it.

qa.q: What did Valli see on her way that made her laugh until tears filled her eyes?
qa.a: She saw a young cow whose tail was high in the air, running very fast right in the middle of the road in front of the bus. The driver sounded his horn again and again, but the more he honked the more frightened the cow became and the faster it ran. Valli found it so funny that she laughed and laughed until tears filled her eyes. On the return journey the same cow lay dead by the roadside, which filled her with horror and took away her joy.

qa.q: Why did Valli refuse the cold drink offered by the conductor?
qa.a: Because she had only sixty paise with her and wanted to keep enough for the return journey. Even though she was thirsty, she refused the drink and asked only to be taken back on the same bus. It shows her discipline and her determination to complete the plan she had made.

qa.q: A student writes: “Valli, a girl of eight, took the bus with her mother.” What is wrong with this? Correct it.
a: Valli went **alone**, without telling anyone; that is the point of the story.
She slipped out of the house while her mother was taking an afternoon nap.
She was proud of being eight years and some months old, and calling herself “madam” to the conductor showed her sense of being grown-up.

qa.q: Valli saved her coins for weeks for one journey. Give two lessons that readers can learn from her planning and saving.
a: A goal needs planning: she found out the fare, the time and the distance before she set out.
It needs self-control: she resisted peppermints, toys and the merry-go-round to save sixty paise.
Determination brings results, though she also learns that a journey can teach unexpected lessons.

qa.q: How did Valli plan her first bus journey?
a: Valli was eight and longed to ride the bus that ran between her village and the town six miles away.
She listened carefully to the passengers' talk and to her neighbour to learn the fare, the timings and what the town was like.
She saved every coin she could, resisting the temptation of peppermints and fair-ground toys, and collected sixty paise for the round trip.
She then waited for her mother's afternoon nap, slipped out of the house and boarded the bus as an ordinary passenger, calling herself ‘madam' to the conductor.

qa.q: The cow is alive on the way out and dead on the way back. What does this episode teach Valli, and why does she tell no one about it?
a: The dead cow is Valli's first meeting with death — she learns that life can vanish suddenly, and her joyful mood turns thoughtful for the rest of the ride.
She tells no one because the journey was her secret and the experience too private to share; like all growing up, this lesson is hers alone.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Valli saved sixty paise for her round trip. On the bus, the conductor offered her a cold drink, but she refused.

(a) What was the fare for each way?
(b) Why did Valli refuse the drink?
(c) What quality of hers does this show?
a: (a) Thirty paise one way, so sixty paise for the round trip.
(b) She had no money to spare; she wanted to keep enough for the return journey.
(c) Self-discipline and determination to carry out her plan.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

On the way to town, Valli laughed at a young cow running in front of the bus. On the way back the same cow lay by the roadside.

(a) What was the cow doing when Valli first saw it?
(b) What did she see on the return journey?
(c) How did her mood change?
a: (a) It was running fast in the middle of the road with its tail in the air, and honking only frightened it more.
(b) The cow lay dead and mangled, struck by a fast vehicle.
(c) Her joy turned to silence and horror; she met death for the first time and became thoughtful.

qa.q: Describe what Valli saw on her ride and how her mood changed.
a: From her window she watched the canal, the palm trees, the green fields, the distant hills and the blue sky, which filled her with joy.
She saw a young cow running in front of the bus, frisking and refusing to move, and laughed aloud at it.
On the return journey her mood changed: the same cow lay dead and mangled by the roadside, struck by a fast vehicle.
The sight silenced her happiness; she understood that the world held ugliness and death as well as beauty, which is the knowledge she brings home.

qa.q: How did Valli plan her bus journey? What does this tell you about her?
a: **Planning:** she listened carefully to the conversations of her neighbours and of people who regularly used the bus, and she asked a few discreet questions here and there. From this she learnt that the town was six miles from her village, that the fare was thirty paise one way, and that the trip took forty-five minutes.

**Saving:** she resisted every temptation to buy peppermints, toys and balloons, and finally she even overcame her urge to ride the merry-go-round at the village annual fair, so that she could save sixty paise in all.
**Timing:** she chose to travel on the one o'clock afternoon bus, when her mother took her daily nap, so that she could be back before her mother woke.

**What it shows:** Valli was observant, determined and capable of self-control far beyond her years. She was also proud of being grown up — she resented being treated as a child, and insisted that the conductor call her madam.

qa.q: How does Valli change in the course of the story? Show her growth from fascination to understanding.
a: At the start she is fascinated by the bus and eager to see the town; she has no companions of her own age.
She shows initiative and courage by planning and saving, then going alone.
During the ride she is joyful and proud, calling herself “madam”.
The dead cow brings her face to face with the cruelty of the world, and her mood turns serious.
She keeps her secret and returns home quietly, a little more grown-up than she left.

mcq.a: **(b) eight years and some months** — a detail she is very conscious of.

mcq.q: The fare from Valli's village to the town was: (a) twenty paise (b) thirty paise (c) fifty paise (d) one rupee
mcq.a: **(b) thirty paise one way**, and the journey took forty-five minutes over six miles.

mcq.q: The conductor called Valli: (a) child (b) madam (c) sister (d) little girl
mcq.a: **(b) madam** — hence the title of the story.

mcq.q: Valli slipped out of the house to catch the bus when: (a) her mother was at the market (b) her mother was taking an afternoon nap (c) her father took her (d) it was dark
mcq.a: **(b) her mother was taking an afternoon nap.** She waited for her mother’s afternoon sleep so that she could go without being noticed.

mcq.q: On the return journey Valli saw the cow: (a) grazing in a field (b) standing on the bus (c) lying dead by the roadside (d) being driven home
mcq.a: **(c) lying dead by the roadside.** The cow that had made her laugh had been killed by a fast vehicle.

mcq.q: Valli was: (a) eight years old  (b) ten  (c) twelve  (d) six
mcq.a: **(a) eight years old.** For all her smallness she was a determined and careful planner.

mcq.q: Valli saved what amount for her bus journey? (a) 30 paise  (b) 60 paise  (c) one rupee  (d) two rupees
mcq.a: **(b) 60 paise.** Thirty paise each way, for the round trip from her village to the town and back.

mcq.q: Valli travelled to the town on the: (a) morning bus (b) one o'clock bus (c) evening bus (d) night bus
mcq.a: **(b) one o'clock bus.** She timed it so that she would be back by about a quarter to four, unseen.

title: The Sermon at Benares
short: The Buddha, Kisa Gotami and the lesson of impermanence.
lede: A story about grief. The mustard-seed test is the heart of the answer.
lens: Extracts from Kisa Gotami's search and from the Buddha's sermon; a 5-mark answer on the Buddha's teaching about death.
Know the mustard-seed condition, why Kisa Gotami failed, and the words about the world being afflicted with decay and death.
concepts: **1. The Buddha's early life.** Born a prince named **Siddhartha Gautama**, he was married young and had a son. At about the age of twenty-five, while out hunting, he came upon a **sick man, then an aged man, then a funeral procession, and finally a monk begging for alms**. These four sights so moved him that he left the palace at once and went out in search of enlightenment. He wandered for seven years and finally sat under a **fig (Bo) tree**, where he was enlightened. He then began to teach, and the tree was renamed the **Bo tree**. His first sermon was given at **Sarnath, near Benares**, on the banks of the Ganges, and has been preserved and is the subject of this chapter.

**2. Kisa Gotami's story.** **Kisa Gotami** had an only son, who died. Carrying the dead child, she went from house to house asking for medicine to cure him, and people thought she had lost her senses. At last a man directed her to the Buddha. The Buddha asked her to bring a **handful of mustard seed**, and when she promised to do so, he added the condition: the mustard seed must be taken from a house **where no one has died** — where no son, husband, parent or servant has been lost. Kisa Gotami went from door to door, and in every house someone had died: a father, a daughter, a servant, a slave. By evening she was weary and hopeless, and she sat down and watched the **lights of the city flicker and go out**; the darkness fell and spread. She understood at last the **selfishness of her grief**: she had been thinking only of her own loss, while death is common to all. She took the body of her child to the forest, laid it down, and returned to the Buddha.

**3. The sermon.** The Buddha said: **'Not from weeping nor from grief will anyone obtain peace of mind; on the contrary, his pain will be the greater and his body will suffer. He will make himself sick and pale, and yet the dead are not saved by his lamentation.'** Those who seek peace of mind should **draw out the arrow of lamentation, complaint and grief**; he who has drawn out the arrow and composed himself will obtain peace. The world is **afflicted with death and decay**, therefore the wise do not grieve, having realised the truth of the world. As a **ripe fruit is always in danger of falling**, so mortals, once born, are always in danger of dying. As **vessels made by the potter end by being broken**, so is the life of mortals. The wise, understanding the world, do not grieve. Grieving will not bring peace; it will only increase suffering.

**4. Themes.** **The universality of death** — every family has lost someone. **The futility of excessive grief** — it harms the living and cannot save the dead. **Enlightenment through experience** — the Buddha does not lecture Kisa Gotami; he makes her discover the truth herself. **Detachment and peace of mind.**
tricks: - The Buddha's method is a **test, not a lecture**: the mustard-seed condition makes Kisa Gotami find the answer herself.
- **'Draw out the arrow of lamentation'** is the key image — quote it in any answer about the sermon.
- **Potter's vessels break; ripe fruit falls.** Two similes that carry a full mark each.
mistakes: - Saying the Buddha refused to help Kisa Gotami. He gave her a **condition**, not a refusal.
- Forgetting that the mustard seed had to come from a house **where no one had died** — the condition is the whole point.
- Writing that the sermon was delivered at Bodh Gaya. It was at **Sarnath, near Benares**.

qa.q: Why did Kisa Gotami go from house to house, and what did she discover?
qa.a: Her only son had died, and she went from house to house asking for medicine to cure him. The Buddha told her to bring a handful of mustard seed, but on the condition that it be taken from a house where no one had died. In every house she entered, someone had died — a father, a daughter, a servant — so she could not find a single such house. She discovered that death is common to all, and that her grief had made her blind to the suffering of others.

qa.q: What did the Buddha say about grieving?
qa.a: He said that no one obtains peace of mind from weeping or from grief; on the contrary, the pain will be the greater and the body will suffer, and the person will make himself sick and pale, yet the dead are not saved by his lamentation. Those who seek peace of mind should draw out the arrow of lamentation, complaint and grief, and having drawn it out, they will obtain peace.

qa.q: Explain the meaning of 'the world is afflicted with death and decay, therefore the wise do not grieve'.
qa.a: It means that death and change are built into the world, so no amount of sorrow can prevent them. The wise understand this truth and accept it, so they do not grieve; they realise that lamentation cannot bring back the dead and only harms the living. Accepting the nature of the world is what brings peace of mind.

qa.q: What were the four sights that led the Buddha to leave the palace?
qa.a: While out hunting at the age of about twenty-five, the prince came upon a sick man, then an aged man, then a funeral procession, and finally a monk begging for alms. These four sights showed him sickness, old age, death and renunciation, and moved him so deeply that he left the palace at once in search of enlightenment.

qa.q: A student writes that the Buddha refused to help Kisa Gotami and that the sermon was given at Bodh Gaya. Correct both statements.
a: The Buddha did not refuse; he asked her to bring a handful of mustard seed, with one **condition**: it must come from a house where no one had died.
The sermon is called the Sermon at Benares because it was delivered at Sarnath, near Benares.
The condition was the whole lesson: it led Kisa Gotami to see for herself that death comes to every house.

qa.q: A friend has lost her grandfather and is deeply upset. Using the Buddha’s approach, say how you would console her in three points.
a: Listen to her first and let her speak of her loss, as the Buddha listened to Kisa Gotami.
Gently help her see that death comes to every family, so she is not alone in her grief.
Remind her that grieving cannot bring the person back, and that remembering him with love will bring peace.

qa.q: What did Kisa Gotami learn from the handful of mustard seed?
a: Carrying her dead child from neighbour to neighbour, Kisa Gotami was told to bring mustard seed from a house where no one had ever died.
She went from house to house and everyone was willing to give her seed, but no household was free of death.
She saw that there was not a single house where some beloved one had not died, and understood that death is common to all.
She accepted the truth, stopped grieving, and took her child's body to the cremation ground before returning to the Buddha to become his follower.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

The Buddha said, “Those who seek peace of mind should pull out the arrow of lamentation, and complaint, and grief.”

(a) What is the “arrow”?
(b) What does “pulling it out” mean?
(c) Why does the Buddha use this image?
a: (a) The pain of lamentation, complaint and grief.
(b) Letting go of grief and accepting what has happened.
(c) An arrow that stays in the body goes on hurting; in the same way, grief that is held on to goes on wounding the mind, so removing it brings peace.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Kisa Gotami carried her dead son from house to house asking for medicine. At last she went to the Buddha.

(a) Why did she carry the dead child with her?
(b) How did the people react to her request for mustard seed?
(c) Why did the Buddha let her find the answer herself?
a: (a) She could not accept that her son was dead and hoped someone could cure him.
(b) Everyone was willing to give the seed, but no house could say that no one had died there.
(c) A truth that one discovers by experience is understood and accepted more deeply than one that is simply told.

qa.q: Describe the Buddha's sermon on death and its message.
a: The Buddha told Kisa Gotami that the life of mortals in this world is troubled and brief and combined with pain; there is no means by which those who are born can avoid dying.
He said that a man is like a potter's earthen vessel: the vessels end in being broken, and so does mortal life.
Both young and adult, both those who are fools and those who are wise, all fall into the power of death; the only escape is to accept it and to live wisely.
He asked her not to grieve, because weeping and complainers gain nothing; only a man who does not tremble at death and does not grieve finds peace.

qa.q: How did the Buddha make Kisa Gotami understand the nature of death without preaching to her?
a: He did not tell her the truth directly. He asked her to bring him a handful of mustard seed — a simple request that gave her hope.
He then added one condition: the mustard seed must be taken from a house where no one had died, where no son, husband, parent or servant had been lost.

Kisa Gotami went from door to door with confidence, but in the first house she was told the father had died; in the next, a daughter; then a servant, then a slave. There was no house untouched by death.

By evening she was tired and hopeless. She sat and watched the lights of the city being lit and then going out until darkness covered everything, and she realised the selfishness of her grief — she had been absorbed in her own loss while death is common to all.

So the Buddha's method was to let her **experience** the truth rather than hear it, which is why it changed her completely. She took her child's body to the forest and returned to him ready to listen.

qa.q: What lessons does the Buddha’s sermon offer for dealing with loss today? Give five points.
a: Death is common to all; no person or family is spared.
Grief, however deep, cannot bring the dead back and only harms the living.
A person is helped more by understanding than by advice, as Kisa Gotami learned by her own search.
Seeing other people’s sorrow makes us more compassionate and less alone.
Acceptance of change brings peace of mind, and that is the wisdom to which the wise hold.

mcq.q: The Buddha asked Kisa Gotami to bring mustard seed from a house where: (a) there was no poverty (b) no one had died (c) everyone was happy (d) there were no children
mcq.a: **(b) no one had died** — a condition no house could meet.

mcq.q: The Buddha gave his first sermon at: (a) Bodh Gaya (b) Kushinagar (c) Sarnath, near Benares (d) Kapilavastu
mcq.a: **(c) Sarnath, near Benares**, on the banks of the Ganges.

mcq.q: The prince Siddhartha Gautama was enlightened under a: (a) sal tree (b) fig (Bo) tree (c) banyan tree (d) mango tree
mcq.a: **(b) fig (Bo) tree**, which was afterwards renamed the Bo tree.

mcq.q: The Buddha asked Kisa Gotami to bring mustard seed from a house in which: (a) no one had ever been sick (b) there was no child (c) no one had ever died (d) there was a physician
mcq.a: **(c) no one had ever died.** The condition revealed to her that death visits every house.

mcq.q: According to the Buddha’s sermon, the lives of mortals are like: (a) a potter’s earthen vessels, which end by being broken (b) a river that flows to the sea (c) a flame that never dies (d) a tree that keeps growing
mcq.a: **(a) a potter’s earthen vessels, which end by being broken.** He compares human life to clay vessels, which are all eventually broken.

mcq.q: Kisa Gotami was asked to bring mustard seed from a house: (a) where no one had died  (b) where a child had been born  (c) where a wedding was held  (d) that belonged to a king
mcq.a: **(a) where no one had died.** She could not find one, and that was the lesson.

mcq.q: The Buddha delivered his first sermon at: (a) Sarnath near Benares  (b) Kushinagar  (c) Lumbini  (d) Bodh Gaya
mcq.a: **(a) Sarnath near Benares.** The deer park there is also called Rishipattan.

mcq.q: The Buddha compared mortal life to: (a) ripe fruits that may fall and earthen vessels fashioned by the potter that must all end broken (b) a river (c) a mountain (d) a lamp
mcq.a: **(a) ripe fruits that may fall and earthen vessels fashioned by the potter that must all end broken.** Both similes teach that death is the common end.

title: The Proposal
short: Chekhov's one-act farce about oxen meadows and hunting dogs.
lede: A play, not a story. Learn who says what, and never lose sight of the fact that the marriage proposal is never actually discussed.
lens: Extracts with a question on character or on the comedy; the two quarrels are the set 5-mark answer.
Know the three characters, the two disputes (**the Oxen Meadows**, then **Squeezer and Guess**), and the ages (**Lomov is 35, Natalya is 25**).
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Stepan Stepanovich Chubukov**, a wealthy landowner, is sitting in his drawing room in his house clothes. **Ivan Vassilevitch Lomov**, his neighbour, arrives dressed in evening clothes with gloves. Chubukov assumes he has come to borrow money, and complains that Lomov always comes to him for a loan. Lomov, nervous and stammering, asks permission to speak. Chubukov embraces him, thinking he has come to borrow money. Lomov then says that he has come to trouble him with a request — and Chubukov again thinks of money. Finally Lomov says that he has come to ask for the hand of **Natalya Stepanovna**, Chubukov's daughter. Chubukov is overjoyed, embraces and kisses him, and calls Natalya in. Before he can propose, Lomov and Natalya fall into a quarrel about the **Oxen Meadows**: Natalya claims the meadows belong to her, and Lomov insists they are his, saying his aunt's grandmother gave the free use of the meadows in perpetuity to the peasants of Chubukov's grandfather in return for making bricks. The argument grows, Chubukov joins in and insults Lomov, and Lomov leaves in a rage. Chubukov then reveals that Lomov had actually come to propose, and Natalya, realising this, begs her father to bring him back. Lomov returns, half-fainting, and Chubukov hurries the two into marriage. But before the proposal is settled, a second quarrel breaks out about hunting dogs — whether **Squeezer** (Lomov's dog) or **Guess** (Chubukov's) is the better dog — and the two men abuse each other again. Lomov collapses, and Chubukov blesses the couple: **'She's willing! Well, I'm sure enough!'** The play ends with the proposal achieved and the argument still going on.

**2. Characters.** **Lomov** — 35, a hypochondriac who suffers from palpitations, a twitching eyebrow and sleeplessness; timid, easily flustered and argumentative. **Chubukov** — loud, short-tempered and money-minded, but ready to push his daughter into a marriage. **Natalya Stepanovna** — 25, spoiled, quarrelsome and more interested in winning an argument than in marriage.

**3. The comedy.** The humour comes from the **contrast between the occasion and the behaviour**: a marriage proposal becomes a shouting match about a piece of land and then about a dog. Nobody ever speaks about love. Chekhov is satirising the **landowning class**, for whom property and possessions matter more than human feeling.
**4. Themes.** The **absurdity of the marriage market**; **greed and property**; **petty pride**; and the fact that people in a hurry to marry are not necessarily in love.
tricks: - **Two quarrels, one proposal that is never discussed.** That is the whole play in one line.
- **Lomov's ailments:** palpitations, twitching eyebrow, sleeplessness, numbness in the leg — a hypochondriac.
- The **Oxen Meadows** argument is about free use in perpetuity granted by an aunt's grandmother — the absurd chain of ownership is part of the joke.
mistakes: - Calling *The Proposal* a story by G. L. Fuentes. It is a **one-act play by Anton Chekhov**.
- Reversing the order of the quarrels: **Oxen Meadows first, then the dogs**.
- Saying Chubukov refuses the match. He is **delighted** and pushes it through, blessing the pair at the end.

qa.q: Why does Chubukov think Lomov has come to him?
qa.a: Because Lomov had come to him the previous year to borrow money, and Chubukov expects the same again. He even complains that Lomov is always coming to him for a loan, and when he hears that Lomov has a request, he assumes it is for money. Only when Lomov asks for Natalya's hand does Chubukov understand.

qa.q: What is the Oxen Meadows quarrel about?
qa.a: It is about who owns the Oxen Meadows, which lie between Lomov's Burnt Marsh and Chubukov's birchwood. Natalya insists the meadows are hers; Lomov says they are his, arguing that his aunt's grandmother gave the peasants of Chubukov's grandfather the free use of the meadows in perpetuity in return for their making bricks for her. The peasants had used them for forty years and regarded them as their own, but neither side will give way, and the argument turns into an exchange of insults.

qa.q: Describe Lomov's character.
qa.a: Lomov is a thirty-five-year-old landowner who is timid, nervous and easily flustered. He is a hypochondriac: he complains of palpitations, a twitching right eyebrow, sleeplessness and numbness in his leg. He is also stubborn and quick to quarrel, which is why a marriage proposal turns into two arguments. Yet he is sincere in his wish to settle down, and he finally gets what he came for.

qa.q: How does the play end? Comment on the ending.
qa.a: Lomov collapses after the argument about the dogs, and Chubukov, without waiting for anything to be settled, blesses the couple and cries that Natalya is willing, calling for champagne. Natalya does not object, and the proposal is agreed. The ending is comic because the marriage is decided in the middle of a quarrel that neither side has stopped fighting — nobody has spoken a word about love, and the audience is left to see how absurd the whole arrangement is.

qa.q: A student writes: “The Proposal is a short story by G. L. Fuentes in which Chubukov refuses to let Natalya marry Lomov.” Correct both errors.
a: *The Proposal* is a **one-act play (a farce) by Anton Chekhov**; G. L. Fuentes wrote “A Letter to God”.
Chubukov does not refuse: he is delighted at the proposal and, at the end, blesses the couple and calls for champagne.
The quarrels over Oxen Meadows and the dogs nearly spoil the match, but they end in agreement.

qa.q: Lomov complains of palpitations, a twitching eyebrow and a numb leg whenever he is excited. What does this show about him and how does it add to the humour?
a: It shows that he is nervous, timid and a hypochondriac who worries too much about his health.
His complaints come at the most tense moments, so his body seems to react whenever he is upset.
This exaggeration makes him comic and adds to the farce.

qa.q: How does ‘The Proposal' satirise the landed gentry?
a: Instead of a romantic proposal, the play shows two neighbours quarrelling over a strip of land and two dogs.
Lomov, a wealthy landowner, comes to ask for Natalya's hand but cannot keep from arguing about Oxen Meadows and about Squeezer and Guess.
Both Chubukov and his daughter lose their temper, shout, and even insult each other's families, while Lomov's real business is forgotten.
Chekhov mocks the vanity, greed and ill-temper of the gentry, for whom property and dogs matter more than affection, and who are ready to marry for convenience.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

The second quarrel in the play is about two dogs, Lomov’s Squeezer and Chubukov’s Guess.

(a) Whose dog is each?
(b) What are the two sides arguing?
(c) What does the quarrel show about the characters?
a: (a) Squeezer belongs to Lomov; Guess belongs to Chubukov.
(b) Each insists that his own dog is better and more valuable and can hunt better.
(c) That the landowners are proud and petty: they fight over trivial things even when a marriage is at stake.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A farce is a comedy with exaggerated characters, absurd situations and quick action.

(a) Give two features of farce in *The Proposal*.
(b) Which character’s weakness is most exaggerated?
(c) Why might Chekhov have used farce to criticise people?
a: (a) A marriage proposal becomes two quarrels; and the characters shout, faint and make up in a hurry.
(b) Lomov’s hypochondria: the palpitations and numb leg.
(c) Laughter exposes their faults gently but clearly; the audience sees how silly the landed gentry’s pride and greed are.

qa.q: Describe the three quarrels in the play and how the proposal is finally made.
a: First quarrel: over Oxen Meadows, which Lomov says belonged to his aunt's grandmother and Natalya claims for her family.
Second quarrel: over the dogs — Lomov's Squeezer and Chubukov's Guess, and whose dog is worth more and can hunt better.
Third quarrel: after Lomov faints and recovers, Chubukov simply tells Natalya to agree, and Lomov's hypochondria and palpitations are brought up.
Chubukov finally forces the proposal through, blesses the couple and hurries them to be married before they quarrel again; the ending is deliberately comic, not romantic.

qa.q: How does Chekhov use the two quarrels to create comedy and to criticise the characters?
a: **The first quarrel, about the Oxen Meadows,** begins before Lomov has even made his proposal. Natalya claims the meadows are hers, Lomov insists they are his, and both become abusive, calling each other a land grabber and an intriguess. Chubukov joins in, calls Lomov an old rat and a Jesuit, and orders him out of the house. The absurdity is that a marriage proposal has become a land dispute, and that Chubukov does not know what the proposal was until after the quarrel.

**The second quarrel, about the dogs,** follows immediately. Lomov praises his dog Squeezer; Chubukov insists his own Guess is better, and they argue over whether Squeezer's muzzle is short, whether Guess is purebred, and whether Squeezer's legs are crooked. The two men become hysterical and Lomov collapses.

**The criticism:** Chekhov shows that for these landowners, property and possessions matter far more than human relationships. Neither Lomov nor Natalya says a word about love or about each other's feelings, and the marriage is arranged in the middle of an argument. The comedy exposes a class that treats marriage as a transaction.

qa.q: Compare the characters of Natalya and Chubukov, showing how each behaves during the play.
a: Natalya is proud and quick-tempered: she insists that Oxen Meadows are hers and argues about the dogs.
She is also eager to be married: when she learns that Lomov came to propose, she is upset that he left and calls him back.
Chubukov is welcoming when he thinks Lomov has come to propose, becomes abusive in the quarrel, and again is eager when the match seems possible.
Both are stubborn about property and pride, and both quickly change their mood.
This makes them comic: their feelings follow their interests, not reason.

mcq.q: 'The Proposal' is a one-act play written by: (a) Anton Chekhov (b) Betty Renshaw (c) Gavin Maxwell (d) Liam O'Flaherty
mcq.a: **(a) Anton Chekhov**, the Russian dramatist.

mcq.q: The second quarrel in the play is about: (a) the Oxen Meadows (b) two hunting dogs (c) money (d) Natalya's age
mcq.a: **(b) two hunting dogs** — Lomov's Squeezer and Chubukov's Guess.

mcq.q: Lomov suffers from: (a) asthma (b) palpitations and a twitching eyebrow (c) a limp (d) poor eyesight
mcq.a: **(b)** — he is a hypochondriac who complains of palpitations, a twitching eyebrow, sleeplessness and numbness in his leg.

mcq.q: “The Proposal” was written by: (a) G. L. Fuentes (b) Anton Chekhov (c) Frederick Forsyth (d) Henri Fabre
mcq.a: **(b) Anton Chekhov.** Chekhov, a Russian writer, wrote this one-act farce.

mcq.q: The two subjects of the quarrels in the play are: (a) a wedding gift and a horse (b) Oxen Meadows and the dogs Squeezer and Guess (c) a house and a river (d) a debt and a letter
mcq.a: **(b) Oxen Meadows and the dogs Squeezer and Guess.** The first quarrel is over who owns Oxen Meadows and the second over whose dog is better.

mcq.q: ‘The Proposal' was written by: (a) Anton Chekhov  (b) Guy de Maupassant  (c) Oscar Wilde  (d) George Bernard Shaw
mcq.a: **(a) Anton Chekhov.** It is a one-act farce, first performed in 1888–89.

mcq.q: Lomov wants to marry Natalya mainly because: (a) she is an excellent housekeeper and he is thirty-five and needs a settled life  (b) he loves her  (c) his father insists  (d) she is very rich
mcq.a: **(a) she is an excellent housekeeper and he is thirty-five and needs a settled life.** His reasons are practical, not romantic, which is the joke.

mcq.q: The first quarrel in the play is about: (a) the Oxen Meadows (b) the two hunting dogs (c) the proposal itself (d) money
mcq.a: **(a) the Oxen Meadows.** The disputed strip of land between the two estates starts the first explosion.
